2. The plaintiff, Trading Corporation of Bangladesh, a statutory body with its Head Office in Dhaka in Bangladesh, alleged that it imported a consignment of 5103.549 Metric Tons(Net) of Galvanised Corrugated Iron Sheets at C & F Chittagong value U.S. $ 41,90,705.35 on the basis of contract No.T.C.B/lMP-2256/88 dated March 21, 1988 read with Memorandum of Understanding dated May 11, 1988 made between the plaintiff and the supplier M/s. Duferco Brazil Limited, London represented by their local Agent Messers Business International Limited of 146/A, New Baily Road, Dhaka, Bangladesh and the Commercial Invoice No.1 158 dated August 2, 1988 of Messers Duferco Brazil Limited, London, after opening letter of Credit No. FFB/LC/ SEM/DLR/152/88ffCB/06 dated March 24, 1988 with Janata Bank, Dhaka, Bangladesh. It further alleged that the consignment was received by the defendant No.1 the ship M.V. CORINA and as loaded on to her at the Port of Piornbina, Italy and that a Bill of Lading No.1 dated July 31, 1988 was issued on behalf of the Defendant No.2 Master of the Vessel for safe carriage to and discharge at' the Port of Chittagong. The consignment was insured with pro-forma defendant No.5 Sadharan Bima Corporation covering various risk of loss under Marine Cargo Policy No. DAC/C/MP-229/88 in lieu of cover Note No. DAC/C/MC-098/83(open) for an amount of Taka 13,82,93,277.00. The plaintiff alleged that while it was anxiously awaiting the arrival of the Cargoes at the Port of destination on receipt a letter dated September 21, 1988 of M/s. Business International Limited, the local agent of the supplier and from a copy of Telex Message dated September 20,1988 of defendant No.3 Patina Shipping Company Ltd., owner of the Vessel, addressed to the local agent of the supplier it learnt that the propeller shaft of defendant No.1 vessel M.V. CORINA sustained severe damage resulting failure of propelling power for which it might not be possible for her to reach the port of destination without salvage/towage and that the ship owner defendant No.3 appointed salvor and declared general average. The plaintiff on receipt of the Telex Massage also from Poseidon Average Adjusters (London) Ltd. dated September 21 and 23,' 1988 came to learn that a general average adjuster was appointed by the ship owner and that the tug "SUHALLI" was engaged to salvage/towage the defendant No.1 vessel from Indian Ocean South of Yamen to the port of destination at Chittagong. The plaintiffs further allegation was that Salvor was unwilling to do the salvage work of the defendant No1 Vessel M.V.CORINA with the cargoes of the plaintiff on board. It also alleged that as the General Average Adjuster threatened the plaintiff that they would not deliver the Cargoes without salvage security and the general average guarantee the plaintiff in the aforesaid circumstances had to arrange. for furnishing security for salvage and the general average guarantee amounting to U.S. $5,80,000.00 equivalent to Taka 1,91,40,000.00 by M/s. TYSER & CO, re-insurance broker of Sadharan Bima Corporation, the Pro-defendant No.5, on behalf of the, plaintiff for the safe delivery of the cargoes worth of Tk. about 14 cores from the vessel and the plaintiff also signed a letter of Counter-Guarantee in favour of the pro-defendant No.5 undertaking to refund such General Average Contribution as might not be payable under the terms of insurance. The plaintiff alleged that it is not at all liable to contribute any amount for such expense which is particular average loss and that they had suffered loss of the aforesaid amount due to furnishing salvage security and general average guarantee. The salvage contractor had already made demand for the encashment of the guarantee and in the event of the defendant No.1 going out of the tidal water of Bangladesh land out of the jurisdiction of this Admiralty Court the plaintiff will have no remedy other than the remedy sought for in the plaint. 

 7. As the arguments advanced by the learned Counsels center round of jurisdiction of this court it would be rather profitable to see the law in force in Bangladesh governing the field. This brings me to trace the origin of the Admiralty Jurisdiction of this Court. The Admiralty jurisdiction may be traced back from the Charter of 1774. Clause 26 of the Charter empowered the Supreme Court of Judicature, at Fort-William in Bengal, amongst others to hear examine, try and determine maritime causes and all matters relating to, amongst others, demands, civil and maritime, whatsoever, between the merchants owners, proprietors of the ship and vessels etc. The said clause empowered the Supreme Court to exercise its Admiralty jurisdiction in the same manner and to the same extent as was exercised by the Courts in England. It continued to exercise such jurisdiction on the strength of clauses 31 and 32 of the Letters Patent of 1862 and 1865 respectively. In course of time the Letter Patent fell in disuse. However, subsequently in order to avoid conflicts between the different courts in England exercising admiralty jurisdiction and to bring about uniformity between the Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts in British possession, the British Parliament enacted the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890 followed by the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) 1891. The latter Act declared the High Court of judicature at Fort William in Bengal as the Colonial Court of Admiralty and empowered it to exercise the same jurisdiction as was exercised by the High Court of England under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. In British India this jurisdiction continued both under Government of India Act, 1915 and the Government Act of 1935. After In dependence in 1947 the High Courts (Bengal) Order 1947 was passed. And paragraph 5 of the said Order provided that the High Court of East Bengal shall have all such original and appellate and other jurisdiction as was exercised by the High Court of Calcutta. After emergence of Bangladesh as an Independent State the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) 1891, has been revised by Bangladesh Laws (Revision and Declaration) Act, 1973 and kept alive. In Albert David-Vs-M/s. Needled Lignin, 34 DLR, 356 we find a learned discourse in this regard by M.H. Rahman, J (As his Lordship then was) while dealing with the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in following words: 

 "The jurisdiction of this court is not derived from the Letters Patent of 1862 or that of 1865, but from the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) of 1891 of England. The latter Act is not on our statute book but it is administered in view of the combined operation of sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890 of the British Parliament and the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India), the later Act being revised by the Bangladesh Laws (Revision and Declaration) Act, 1973 (Act VIII of 1973) is now on our statute book. It is true that if the revised Court of Admiralty Act of 1891 is read in isolation then it would not give any idea as to the nature and extent of the Admiralty jurisdiction of this court but it is to be read in its historical perspective. Under the Act of 1891 the High Court Division of this Court was declared as the Court of Admiralty. This court exercises the same jurisdiction as the High Court of England exercised in 1890 under the Admiralty Court Act of 1861." 

 8. Mr. M. Hafizullah also referred me to the decision in the case of Kings Shipping Trading Co Vs. M/s. L.S. Line, 38 DLR, 30 in support of his contention that this Court exercises its Admiralty Jurisdiction derived from Admiralty Act, 1861 and docs not exercise the same jurisdiction as is being exercised by the Admiralty Court in England under Administration of Justice Act, 1956 passed by the British Parliament. In delivering the judgment of the report Sultan Hossain Khan, J. observed : 

 "The Admiralty Court of England exercises jurisdiction on the basis of statute laws. The court similarly exercises jurisdiction as has been given to it under section 6 of the Act of 1861 by virtue of the provision of section 2(2) of Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and as such Administration of Justice Act, 1956 is not applicable in Bangladesh. 

 9. In view of the aforesaid judicial pronouncements I have no hesitation to hold that the Admiralty Court of the High Court Division derives its jurisdiction from Admiralty Court Act1861 as has been made it applicable by virtue of Section 2 (2) of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890. 

 10. Now let us revert to the contentions at the Bar on the question of jurisdiction to entertain the suit and to issue of the warrant of arrest of the vessel M. V. CORINA. This requires a close examination of the relevant provision of law. Mr. Hafizullah placing reliance on section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 submits that the claim of the cargo owners does only arise out of damage done to the goods or any part thereof by negligence or misconduct or for any breach of duty or breach of contract on the part of the owner, or craw of the ship. He continues to argue that the plaintiff not having had alleged any damage done to the cargoes and the cargoes having already had taken delivery by the plaintiff, the suit is not maintainable in Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court. On the other hand, the learned counsel for the petitioner submits that this court has jurisdiction to entertain the plaint and pass the decree sought for inasmuch as the plaintiff has no liability to contribute towards the general average loss as the ship owner failed to ensure the seaworthiness of the ship and to man, equip and supply her properly for safe adventure. He submits that as such failure on the part of the ship owner is a breach of duty or breach of contract and the damage in question was due to the negligence of the master of the ship and alleged general average loss incurred for the salvage or towage of the ship being the absolute liability of the ship owner, this Admiralty Court has jurisdiction to entertain the plaint and to issue warrant of arrest or detention of the vessel M.V.CORINA. Therefore, he submits that the order of warrant and the arrest of the ship 1 M.V.CORINA is quite maintainable. This leads me to examine the pleading. From reading the pleading it seems to me that the claim is based on the loss to be incurred by the plaintiff for contributing to general average loss declared by the ship owners. There is no allegation as to damage of cargo, no allegation as to delay and deviation or fall in. the price of the cargo. According to Mr. M. Hafizullah the loss alleged in this case does not relate to the claim for damage done to goods within the meaning of section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. Section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 reads: 

 11. Mr. Kamal in support of his contention referred me to the decision in the case of Al-sayer Navigation Co-Vs-Delta International Traders Ltd. 34 DLR(AD)110 and argues that the power of the Admiralty jurisdiction of the court has been widened and the present suit being a suit for compensation for the loss of money suffered due to declaration of general average by the ship owner the present suit is maintainable. He relied upon the following passage of the report: "Thereafter by section 49 of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956, section 22 of 1925 Act was repealed and by section 87 the Admiralty jurisdiction was conferred the power to hear and determine" any of the following questions of claims" :- 

 "Any claim arising out of an agreement relating to the carriage of goods in a ship. 'Thus the jurisdiction was enlarged and all this is required is that the claim must arise out of an agreement of carriage of goods. It is evident there has been some change since 1861. In 1861 the words 'damage' done to the goods' occupied a central place and the words 'breach of duty' or breach of contract' were related to the goods carried into any port in England or Wales but in 1956 Act jurisdiction was conferred to hear and determine any claim arising out of any arrangement relating to the carriage of goods in ship." 

 12. As the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Division is exercised by virtue of Admiralty Courts Act, 1861 read with Colonial Courts Act (India) 1891, provisions of section 6 of Admiralty Court Act, 1861 is the relevant law so far as it relates to the present dispute. According to section 6 of the said Act as quoted above the Admiralty Court of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh can only exercise its jurisdiction over any claim for damage done to the goods or any part thereof by the negligence or misconduct of or for any breach of duty or breach of contract on the part of the owner, master or crew of the ship. In this instant case, as it appears from the written objection (Vide paragraph No. 6) the vessel was seaworthy and she suffered damage due to "sand gaining access into stern tube when the vessel touched bottom passing through Suez Canal." The petitioner's case is also that "the damage alleged to have been caused to the defendant No. 1 M.V. CORINA and/or her propeller/Talc shaft was due to her seaworthiness and insufficiency and unsuitability of the men; equipment and supplier." and there is no allegation in the petition that the cargoes suffered any damage, rather the petitioner has admitted that the delivery of the cargoes were taken in full. Thus from the statements made in the petition and the written objection, it seems to me, that the claim for damage is not a claim for the damage of the goods rather the claim rests on the contribution to be made by the petitioner towards the general average loss resulting from the damage suffered by the ship itself. In my view, such a claim does not fall within the mischief of the provision of section 6 of the Admiralty Courts Act, 1861. Now it remains forus to decide whether damage caused to the ship due to "sand gaining access into stern tube when the vessel touched bottom passing through Suez Canal" can be said to be a damage to the goods due to breach of contract or breach of duty. In deciding the point the paramount consideration is whether the damage caused to the ship due to breach of contract or of duty resulted damage of the goods. There being no allegation as to damage of goods, the damage due to "sand gaining access into stern tube when the vessel touched bottom passing through Suez Canal" for which the ship lost her propelling power cannot be equated with the damage to the goods due to breach of contract or breach of duty or negligence or misconduct of the ship owner or the crews as envisaged in section 6 of the Admiralty Courts Act, 1861. In this view of legal position I am of the opinion that the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Division cannot be exercised in deciding the present suit wherein no allegation has been made as to damage of the goods, as contemplated in section 6 of the Admiralty Courts Act, 1861. In this case before me there is no allegation as to damage to the cargo, no allegation as to delay and deviation and no allegation as to loss of price of the cargo when the same was unloaded and delivered to the owner. In absence of any of the said allegation the contention of the learned Counsel of the petitioner that there as breach of contract or of duty on the part of the ship owner or the master is untenable as the allegation regarding breach of contract or breach of duty or negligence or misconduct as a result of which damage is caused to the ship has nothing to do with the damage of goods. Mere allegation of breach of contract or misconduct on the part of the ship owner, the master and the crew of the vessel is not enough to invoke the provision of section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. In order to bring the suit within the ambit of section 6 of the Act the allegations must relate to the damage of the cargoes. But such allegation is conspicuously absent in this case. The Administration of Justice Act, 1956 in England no doubt has widened the scope of the suit and extended the power of the Admiralty Court in England to determine "any claim arising out of an agreement relating to the carriage of goods in a ship" but we cannot give such an extended meaning to the expression damage to the goods or any part thereof appearing in section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. To give such a meaning will be construing the provision of section 6 contrary to the canon of interpretation of statute as the language used in section 6 admits of no ambiguity nor does the language used therein render itself to any other interpretation to bring the expression damage to the goods or any part thereof within the ambit of the words any claim arising out of an agreement relating to the carriage of goods in a ship of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956. A careful reading of the decision in the case of Al Sayer Navigation Co. does not also support the contention of the learned counsel of the plaintiff as in the said decision it has not been held that the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 is applicable in Bangladesh.The decision so far as it relates to the Admiralty jurisdiction of the courts in England, has traced the enlargement of the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court in England from time to time by enactments of the British Parliament.
